scav

how a statechart gets laid out
    Introduction

    What scav is

    scav authors, lays out and renders Harel statecharts. You give it a chart as text and it returns a drawing: every state boxed, every transition routed at right angles, every label placed, and the same bytes on every machine.

    Harel statecharts have no adequate tooling. The incumbents fail on the one thing a statechart has that a flowchart lacks: transitions that cross the borders of nested states. ELK's default hierarchy handling (SEPARATE_CHILDREN) silently drops an edge that skips a containment level, with no route and no warning. Its only fix, INCLUDE_CHILDREN, lays the whole subtree out in one run, which loses each subtree's own direction and aspect ratio, and ELK's maintainer calls it "generally a little bit buggy". PlantUML, whose files scav replaces, has no holistic layout. It lays each composite out on its own and attaches the transitions that leave it afterwards, so its splines sweep diagonally across the drawing and through submachine boxes. It cannot express a transition from any concurrent region but the first to a state outside the composite, so it refuses tcp.scav, one of the charts below. Mermaid documents the limitation, itemis CREATE deleted its auto-layout, and Stately declares layout a non-goal. Of about twenty tools surveyed, none publishes a statechart layout algorithm.

    scav's bet is phase 0. Every transition is cut at each border it crosses into segments, which are joined by ports on those borders. Each submachine then becomes an ordinary flat graph that can be ordered on its own, and a long transition still lands in the right place because its pieces are pinned to the borders it crosses. Earlier tools get one of those two properties or the other, never both.

    The model

    A state may hold submachines, each of which holds more states. A state with at least one submachine is a composite. One with two or more is concurrent: its submachines run at the same time, are drawn side by side with a dashed divider between them, and are informally called regions. A submachine that no state owns is a document root.

    Every state has a kind: Normal, Initial, Final, Choice, Junction, Fork, Join, History or DeepHistory. Everything but Normal is a pseudostate. You reach initial and final only through *: trans * -> X creates an initial state in X's submachine, and trans X -> * creates a final. Layout treats a pseudostate as an ordinary small box sized from the profile's minimum for its kind. On the shipped readable profile an initial or final is 224 × 224 grid units, a choice 320 × 320, and a fork or join bar 64 × 960, standing upright because ranks run left to right. (A grid unit is 1/16 pt; see principles.)

    A transition joins any two states anywhere in the tree. A transition whose ends lie in different submachines is hierarchy-crossing. In ELK's terms, a short hierarchical edge crosses one containment border and a long hierarchical edge crosses more than one. A transition between two regions of one concurrent state is drawn as a direct arrow, not up through the parent, because scav draws topology, not execution paths.

    The model is flat arrays of plain records linked by ordinal, not a graph of objects. Every row records the statement and the include it came from, so any drawn primitive can be traced back to its source bytes. The figure above does the same walk from the chart's text.

    Transition kinds

    A transition's kind (external, internal or local) is an input to layout. It decides whether the arrow crosses the source state's border.

    kindthe source's bordera self-transition
    external (the default)crosseda loop outside the box
    internalnot crossed: the route starts on the border's inner faceno route at all. The application reserves room in the state's text bands and draws it there, as brew does with pressure adjust
    localas internal at the sourceno route

    When the destination encloses the source (Idle -> On from inside On), the route ends on On's inner face whatever the kind.

    The .scav format

    • Terse, keyword-led, LL(1) and whitespace-insensitive. Commas separate every item. The unnamed string after a state or transition is its label.
    • * means initial or final depending on which side of the arrow it is on. s, m and t are aliases for state, submachine and trans, and print back in full.
    • States written directly inside a state's block belong to an unnamed submachine 0. A named block, submachine water { … }, makes one region of a concurrent state.
    • Paths are /-separated and resolve innermost-outward. :name picks a submachine, as in Brewing:water/Heating or arm/Moving:travel/Cruising.
    • include "axis.scav" as arm creates one state arm whose submachine is the included document's root. Including a file twice gives two independent copies.
    • There is one canonical printer, scav fmt. JSON is an output projection, not a format.

    Layout is a library

    scav is a toolkit, not a framework. It owns the model, the layout, and the vocabularies that layout and drawing must agree on: the draw list, space requests and text metrics. It does not own appearance, composition or the render loop. Its main user is a build system: scav render in a docs pipeline, scav fmt --check, scav check. An editor or game tool links the same pieces and supplies its own drawing back end. The interface is a flat extern "C" ABI with five opaque handles, plain structs passed with their sizeof, no callbacks anywhere, and routers chosen by name. It ships as one shared object, libscav, with Python bindings generated from the extracted ABI.

    Layout's only inputs are the model, three integer tables of space requests, and a profile of 52 integer settings. Layout never sees a font or a string. The application measures text with scav's metrics and passes the extents in:

    • BoxSpace{min_w, h_before, h_after} per state and per submachine: the width its text needs, and the bands above and below its children where the name and internal transitions go.
    • PathClear{src, dst} per transition: how far to shorten each end, room for the arrowhead.
    • PathBox{subject, w, h, order}, zero or more per transition: a box layout slides along the route, in other words a label.
    1. The application measures its content with scav's text metrics and fills the three tables.
    2. scav_layout_run validates the profile and the tables (it rejects bad input, never clamps it), lays the chart out, and writes geometry columns (scav.geom.state, route, point, portslot, …) plus one placed rectangle per PathBox.
    3. The application builds a draw list from those columns, optionally with scav's reference builder.
    4. It renders the draw list with scav's SVG back end or its own.
    ScaleThe design target is 2,000 states, 5,000 transitions and nesting 16 deep. The corpus that the rest of this page draws on is eleven hand-written charts, from the 3-state estop to bottler, which nests six levels and sends faults from the innermost valve straight out to the root.
    Principles

    The rules everything else obeys

    A drawing is a pure function of the chart, the space requests and the profile, computed in integers on a fixed grid. The same inputs give the same bytes, whatever the compiler, the platform or the thread count.

    A pure function

    Layout is a function of (model, space requests, profile) and nothing else. There is no quick or polish mode, no warm start from a previous layout, no persisted cache and no hysteresis. scav does keep memos, but a memo is not a cache in that sense. Every memo is keyed on every value the step reads, compared whole, so a hit returns exactly what the computation would have returned. It changes the wall clock and nothing else, like the thread count.

    Stability comes from construction, not from a cost term. Each stage preserves order, every tie is broken by a total order, and document order drives reading order. The limit is stated plainly: a one-state change can still flip a choice and cascade through the drawing. The remedy is an author's pin or hint, not a memory of the last layout. Earlier designs had a stability weight, a prior layout and dirty regions, and all were removed for this reason.

    The integer grid

    All layout arithmetic is integer. Coordinates are in grid units of 1/16 pt, a compile-time constant. Coordinates are int32 and products int64. The domain is symmetric, |x| ≤ COORD_MAX = 219 − 1 = 524,287, so negating, taking abs or mirroring cannot overflow. Space requests and spacing fields are capped at COORD_MAX / 4 because the box formula adds several of them. Rectangles are half-open, [x0, x1) × [y0, y1), and output is root-absolute, applied as one final pass. <cmath> is banned in layout, because libm differs between platforms. Square roots are an integer isqrt, ratios are compared by cross-multiplying, and an intersection test is four orient2d sign checks, never a constructed point.

    The 2,000-state stress chart measures 167,194 × 109,253 grid units under the real font, about 3× inside the domain. If real charts ever outgrow it, the grid goes to 1/8 pt rather than widening the integers.

    The determinism contract

    "Layout output is a function of the C++ abstract machine, not of any implementation." Any conforming C++20 toolchain must produce the same bytes. The evidence matrix is six toolchain triples (clang, gcc and MSVC over libc++, libstdc++ and the MSVC STL, on macOS, Linux and Windows) × Debug, Release and a test build × 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and 16 threads. Odd and prime thread counts are mandatory, because they expose reduction-order bugs that powers of two hide.

    • The thread count never reaches the output. Work is cut into shards whose count depends only on the model: clamp(bit_ceil(ceil_div(entities, 64)), 1, 256). One process-wide pool runs them, and the first free thread claims the lowest unclaimed shard of the deepest open job. A shard writes only its own slot, and reductions merge slots in index order, so which thread ran a shard changes only the wall clock.
    • Reductions are associative, though not necessarily commutative: argmin(value, index) and list append qualify because index order makes them well defined. Saturating addition is banned because it is not associative.
    • Every comparator is a total order ending in a stable key derived from the input: "ties are forks". Any sort that reaches the output is a vendored stable merge sort; std::sort is banned in layout.
    • Randomness, where any is used, is stateless and addressed by position: rnd(seed, phase, item, step). Its only consumer is a test-only delay injector. The search uses no randomness at all.
    • A closed list of banned constructs: types whose width varies (int, long, size_t in value computation), std::hash, iterating unordered containers (scav's HashMap has no begin(), so doing so is a compile error), pointer-keyed containers, <random>, raw / and % on possibly negative values, <cmath>, hashing structs with padding, locale-aware formatting, bitfields, out-of-range shifts and unchecked narrowing.

    Two measurement scales

    scav's numbers come in two scales, and they are never compared across. No-text means no space requests at all: every state at its minimum size and no labels. The committed cost goldens (corpus_cost.txt) and the unit tests use it. Real text means text measured with the bundled font: this is what scav render, scav dump --layout, the audit tool and corpus_cost_measured.txt use, and what every other drawing on this page shows. The two scales lay out different problems. Text widens states and gaps, label terms are zero under no-text, and the search lands on different pins. A number carried from one scale to the other checks nothing.

    Two rules from review"What is trivially right is construction, not search": a straight line beats a kinked one, a start state sits beside the state it enters, and a route never runs along a border. These are built in, not left for the search to discover. And "every rule gets an isolated test on a trivial layout": each rule is held by a chart small enough to name every route.
    Overview

    The pipeline at a glance

    Four phases turn a chart into a drawing: decompose, order, size and route. Labels and a cost follow. A search wraps the whole run and evaluates hundreds of thousands of variations of it, keeping the cheapest.

    Each phase is its own translation unit, and it hands the next phase a plain struct declared in its header. None of these intermediates crosses the ABI. Every phase also reads the chart for containment and liveness, but never for something an earlier phase computed, so a unit test can type a phase's input in directly: "a SubmachineOrders with three ranks is nine integers typed into a test".

    stagereadsproduces
    phase 0, decomposethe charta split graph: every transition cut into segments at the borders it crosses, with a port at each crossing
    phase 1, ordersplit graph, label sizes, sweep_count, pinsper frame (one submachine's graph): each node's rank (its column) and position within the rank, chained long edges, gap charges for labels
    phase 2, sizeorders, space requests, spacing, aspect targetevery state, band and submachine rectangle, root-absolute, folded and packed bottom-up
    facing passorders and the first sizingports turned to face their route's far end. If any turned, phases 1 and 2 run again
    phase 3, routeorders, sizing, arrowhead trims, router, face pinsorthogonal polylines, port slots, then placed labels
    cover and costroutes and sizingthe chart rectangle grown over every route point and label, then the lexicographic Cost

    One pass from ordering through cost, for one setting of the search's choices, is one candidate. Phase 1 reads no extents from the profile, only sweep_count and the line height (and the label sizes from the space requests), so its first run is hoisted: it runs once per layout under the caller's profile and is shared by all sixteen whole-chart variations and every inflation retry. A pin is a choice the search fixes, such as which rank a state sits in or which face a route leaves by. When the search tries a pin, the candidate re-derives every phase the pin reaches, copying any frame whose inputs did not change.

    The search around it

    1. Validate the profile, the space tables and the router name, and reject on failure.
    2. Decompose once, and order once.
    3. Level 2: 16 rows, each a whole-chart setting of four phase-2 knobs (whether the packer also tries a one-row box packing, whether packing compacts, which aspect each frame packs toward, whether long rank runs always fold). Every row runs one candidate, in parallel.
    4. Level 1 from every viable row: steepest descent over pins, one move per round, until no move improves.
    5. Kicks: structural changes (reverse a cycle edge, turn a frame to run down the page, flip a fold), each searched to convergence and kept only if it ends cheaper. Then a refold search.
    6. Take the cheapest row (ties go to the lower row), and write the geometry columns, placed labels and diagnostics.

    On mill, the largest corpus chart, one layout scores about 1.6 to 1.9 million candidates. The search and fast sections explain how.

    When routing fails: the inflation retry

    The inflation retry lives inside one candidate. If routing reports a net that is unreachable (no path even with zero clearance), it raises rank_sep, node_sep and sub_sep by 32 units (2 pt) on a copy of the profile, cumulatively, and re-runs phases 2 and 3 from the same ordering, up to 8 times. It keeps the attempt that degraded least (ties to the earliest) and stops at the first attempt where everything routes. Only unreachable triggers it. A frame too large for the router or an end outside its region does not move with spacing, so those never trigger it. The cost is always scored under the caller's profile, and the inputs digest hashes the caller's profile, so a retry cannot move a golden. Level 1 never accepts a candidate that inflated: "a move that only fits once the whole chart's spacing was widened is not a better placement, it is a bigger drawing." Whatever still fails is drawn as a straight line and reported with one RouteDegraded diagnostic per transition, and the run still succeeds. The corpus and both 2,000-state stress charts inflate zero times.

    Where a candidate's time goesOn mill with no text, one candidate took about 145 µs at one measured commit: ordering 17, sizing 42, routing 55 and cost 30. Real text adds about 94 µs of label placement.
    Phase 0

    Decompose: frames, segments, ports

    Before anything is placed, every transition is cut at each border it crosses. What is left is one ordinary flat graph per submachine, and those graphs are joined only at ports on the borders.

    A frame is one submachine laid out as its own layered graph: each region of a concurrent state, each composite's submachine and each document root. The frame is the unit that is ordered, sized, sharded across threads and reused between candidates. From a parent frame's point of view a composite state is a plain node; what is inside it is another frame's business.

    A transition whose ends lie in different frames is split at every containment border it crosses. Each piece is a segment lying in exactly one frame, and each cut is a port on the crossed state's border. This turns ELK's long-hierarchical-edge problem into one-dimensional port ordering along each composite's sides. It is also what makes a long edge pull on every level it passes: one port per crossed border, so a state 16 levels deep with an edge to the top constrains every frame in between, with no weight needed.

    How a transition is split

    1. Dead transitions are skipped. An internal or local self-transition gets no segments at all, because it has no route.
    2. Build each end's chain of ancestors, innermost first, and strip the part they share.
    3. If the source encloses the destination, an internal or local transition starts on the source's inner face, and an external one leaves the source's border and re-enters it.
    4. Exit the source's chain from innermost to outermost. The source itself is exited only by an external transition.
    5. If the two chains diverge into different submachines of one state, cross the separator between those regions instead of that state's border. That middle segment is routed inside the owning state, in the source region's frame.
    6. Enter the destination's chain from outermost to innermost. If the destination encloses the source, end on its inner face.
    7. Walk the crossings: one port per crossing, and one segment per pair of consecutive ends, each in the frame it lies in.

    Each end of a segment is therefore one of three things: a port on a crossed border, the endpoint state's box in this frame, or the endpoint state's inner face (an internal or local source, or a destination that encloses its source). In phase 1 a port that belongs to this frame becomes a boundary node on the frame's edge: exits sit on the trailing border and entries on the leading one.

    Each transition's label belongs to one segment: the one in its lowest common ancestor frame, the innermost submachine holding both ends (for two regions of one state, the separator segment). Ids are stable: a port is (compound state, side, transition, crossing depth) and a segment (transition, ordinal), never derived from how work was sharded.

    Why not lay out the whole tree at onceELK's INCLUDE_CHILDREN does exactly that, and loses each subtree's own direction and aspect. ELK's default instead drops edges that skip a level. Cutting at borders keeps each submachine independently orderable and keeps every long edge, at the price of ports that the later phases must place well. A unit test holds the extreme: an exit from 16 levels deep produces 17 segments and 32 ports.
    RuleA phase never infers what kind of end a segment has from another phase's tables; phase 0 records it. The one defect of that kind drew Idle -> On from On's border to its centre.
    Phase 1

    Ordering: which rank, which slot

    Each frame becomes a layered graph. Phase 1 decides the rank every node sits in (its column) and its slot within that rank. It reads only pins, label sizes, the line height and sweep_count, so it runs once per layout and every candidate the search scores shares it.

    A frame is one submachine laid out on its own. Its graph has three kinds of node (order.cpp:1030-1091): a state node for each live child state, in document order; a boundary node for each segment end that is a port on this frame's border or an inner face; and the bend nodes that chaining adds later. Each segment (the part of a transition inside one frame) becomes one edge. An edge whose two ends resolve to the same node, such as an external self-loop, is dropped. Ranks are columns: they run left to right, nodes stack down within a rank, rank_sep (576, 36 pt) is the gap between columns and node_sep (288) the gap within one. Disconnected components are ordered separately and packed by phase 2; otherwise every unconnected state would sit at rank 0 in one tall column.

    Breaking cycles

    Layering needs a DAG, and statecharts are full of cycles. First, Tarjan's strongly-connected-components pass (iterative, roots in node order) marks every segment whose two ends share a component as cyclic. Only cyclic segments are candidates for the search's reverse move (order.cpp:239-304).

    Then orient_acyclic (order.cpp:309-361) does two things. It applies every reverse pin (a pin is one choice the search fixes; a ReversePin names a segment to flip). Then it runs an iterative depth-first search with roots in node index order (document order) and each node's out-edges in segment order. An edge into a node still on the stack is a back edge: it is flipped and marked reversed. No node moves; only edge directions change.

    RuleWhich edge of a cycle is reversed is an artefact of declaration order. That is why the reversal is a search dimension rather than a rule (§11.10d).

    Ranking by longest path

    assign_ranks (order.cpp:363-437) runs four steps on the DAG:

    1. Topological order by Kahn's algorithm, sources seeded in node order.
    2. Longest path from the sources: in topological order, every edge v → w sets rank[w] = max(rank[w], rank[v] + 1).
    3. Pull right, in reverse topological order: a node that is not a boundary node and has fewer in-edges than out-edges moves to one rank before its nearest successor. A source with three successors therefore sits next to them, not at rank 0. (The PRD does not mention this step.)
    4. Sink boundary nodes to the last rank, so exits sit on the trailing border and entries on the leading one; then empty ranks are squeezed out.

    Rank pins

    A rank pin (RankPin{state, rank}) sets one state's rank directly after ranking (order.cpp:1226-1245). Longest path does not run again, so an edge may end up flat (both ends in one rank) or pointing backward. Initial pseudostates are never pinned. After the pins, each initial is re-seated one rank before the nearest state it touches; if that state is at rank 0, every other node moves up one to make room. Then empty ranks are squeezed. A pin asking for the rank longest path already chose changes nothing (§11.10a).

    Side pins act on ports (order.cpp:1197-1257). A port pinned to a cross border (the top or bottom of a frame that runs across) holds its edge out of ranking, cycle breaking and the sweeps; the port takes its mate's rank and sits first or last in it. A port pinned to a rank border has its edge oriented so the boundary node is the source (leading border) or the sink (trailing border).

    Charges: room the gaps must hold

    Before chaining, while each edge still spans its whole rank range, rank_derived charges each rank boundary (the gap after a rank) with the room it must hold (order.cpp:672-773):

    • Label charge. An edge crossing one boundary charges that gap its label's width (its PathBox width, or its height in a frame running down). An edge crossing several boundaries is placed afterwards, widest label first: it takes the widest boundary it crosses (ties go to the middle), and costs nothing if that boundary already holds it. An edge inside one rank charges nothing.
    • Lane charge. Per connected component, an edge "turns" in its first boundary and, if it spans more than one, in its last. A boundary where two or more edges turn reserves lanes × line height (269 per lane at readable). This goes into the gaps that decide folding only; phase 2 recomputes the real lane room (§11.9.5).

    Textbook label placement adds a dummy node per label. scav widens the gap instead: dummy nodes would double every rank and need a frame to own each label (§11.3).

    Chaining long edges

    Every edge spanning more than one rank becomes a chain through one bend node per intermediate rank (chain_long_edges, order.cpp:439-477). The bends take part in the sweeps like any node, and the router later treats them as hard waypoints (§11.16). A cut (ChainCut{trans, leg}) leaves the segment as one long edge with no bends, so the router draws it freely (§11.10b). That matters: 58 of the corpus's 257 transitions carry a phase-1 bend, and they hold 295 of its 421 kinks (70%).

    Crossing minimisation by median sweeps

    minimize_crossings (order.cpp:587-619) starts from document order: in each rank, pinned-first ports, then states, then boundary nodes, then bends, then pinned-last ports. It runs up to sweep_count = 8 sweeps. Even sweeps go down (ranks 1 to R−1, each ordered by the median of its predecessors' positions); odd sweeps go up (ranks R−2 to 0, by the median of successors').

    • median_of sorts the neighbours' positions and takes the upper median, element size/2. A node with no neighbour on that side has no median; it is a fixed barrier that keeps its slot.
    • reorder_rank swaps adjacent nodes while med[i] > med[i+1], strictly, so ties keep their order.
    • After each sweep the frame's crossings are recounted; the best arrangement so far is kept, and sweeping stops as soon as a sweep reaches 0. A frame that starts at 0 is never swept.

    Crossings are counted per adjacent rank pair: sort the edges by (north position, south position) and count inversions with a Fenwick tree. Edges that share an endpoint never count as crossing (order.cpp:216-234, 500-535).

    Why the medianThe barycenter heuristic has no constant-factor bound (it can be Ω(√n) off); the median has one. Global sifting is a named lever, not built. transpose was built, improved nothing anywhere, and is not in the pipeline; running it inside the sweep loop took the corpus from 0 layered crossings to 7 (§11.3, §11.10). With sweep_count 0 against 8, routed crossings over the corpus were 99 against 91 (no-text), though axis (2 against 4) and mill (38 against 43) did better unswept.

    The sweeps leave little on the table: 1,154 frames over the corpus, the gauntlet and the 2k targets carry zero layered crossings, while the routed drawings of the same charts had 87 (§11.10a, §11.10). The crossings a reader sees are made by routing, not by ordering.

    Orientation, pseudostates and fold pins

    An orient pin (OrientPin, applied by a kick) turns a frame to run down: ranks become rows and the axes swap everywhere downstream (§11.10g step 6; order.cpp:857-859). An initial pseudostate is seated rank_sep before the state it enters and level with it; a final is mirrored after its source (§11.10g step 1). A fold pin (FoldPin) passes through phase 1 untouched: it names where phase 2 cuts a long rank run.

    The real ranks

    The figure below reads brew's shipped drawing from the trace. Its pins include two rank pins (Off to rank 0 and the final $final to rank 1) and one reverse pin (Off → SelfCheck); the DFS flips Brewing → Standby by itself.

    What the search can change here

    Phase 1 is where most of the search's moves land: rank (rank pins), cut (chain cuts), reverse (reverse pins on cyclic segments), side (port sides) and orient (a kick that turns a frame). Fold pins pass through to phase 2. In-rank position is not searched: measured, it has no slack. A candidate copies every frame whose inputs match the incumbent's, so a move re-orders only the frames it touches.

    RejectedEades–Lin–Smyth greedy cycle removal: not adopted, because the search chooses reversals. dot's edge-weight schedule: deliberately not taken (§11.3). One warning from scale: on a flat 2k-state chain, DFS reversal can make edges a thousand ranks long, and chaining them makes a million ordering nodes; without wrapping skips that costs seconds instead of 2 ms (§11.3).
    Phase 2

    Sizing: coordinates, gaps, folds and packing

    Phase 2 turns ranks and slots into rectangles. It works bottom-up: the deepest frames are sized first, their owner states take the frames' sizes, and so on up to the root. Then one top-down pass makes every coordinate root-absolute.

    The loop buckets frames by depth and sizes the deepest, then their owner states, then those states' frames, up to the root frame (size.cpp:2554-2626); a descent then turns submachine-local coordinates into root-absolute ones (size.cpp:2630-2679). Each frame goes through lay_out_sub (layers, Brandes–Köpf, folding, label room) and place_sub; each composite state through size_state, which packs its sibling submachines and applies the box formula. "Bottom-up sizing has no locality: a leaf growing one unit resizes every ancestor to the root" (§11.4).

    Across the ranks: Brandes–Köpf

    Along the ranks, each layer gets an x origin. Across them, each node needs a coordinate: its height on the page in a frame running across. scav uses Brandes–Köpf (BK), linear-time and balanced, once per connected component per fold piece, with sep = node_sep (288) between neighbours, edge to edge (coords.cpp). A node's extent is its cross-axis size plus a label reserve (leader plus label height) for labelled legs. Only edges between consecutive layers count, earlier end first.

    1. Mark type-1 conflicts. A non-inner edge that crosses an inner segment (bend node to bend node) is marked, so long chains stay straight (coords.cpp:343-379).
    2. Four alignment passes: layers walked forward or backward, and each layer walked from its first node or its last (BK's down/up × left/right). In each, a node tries its median neighbour(s) in the layer just walked, positions (d−1)/2 and d/2, and takes the first edge that is unmarked and does not cross an alignment already made in this layer. Aligned nodes form a block that shares one coordinate. Strong edges go first, then weak ones (an initial's edge, a scav extension). Blocks carry per-end port offsets, so a segment is aligned where it meets a composite's port rather than at its centre (§11.10g step 2).
    3. Compaction, with the 2020 erratum (Brandes, Walter, Zink, arXiv:2008.01252; the PRD says "read the erratum", §11.2). Blocks are placed in topological order of the neighbour DAG rather than by the published recursion, each block takes its root's coordinate plus offset exactly once, and class shifts are a separate pass over adjacent class pairs, layer by layer, so a shift accumulates along a critical path (coords.cpp:219-340).
    4. Balance. The four results are aligned to the narrowest one (forward-walked runs by their leading edge, backward ones by their trailing edge); each node then takes the average of its two median values, floor((v[1] + v[2]) / 2) (coords.cpp:414-463).

    Then the alignment rules (§11.10g step 2): states joined by an edge inside one column share one centre line; a state joined to a composite's port is centred on that port; an initial or final pseudostate is seated rank_sep from its mate, level with it. BK was 95–96% of phase 2's time when measured; a per-thread memo keyed on the whole graph returns identical results for a repeated graph. Network simplex placement was tried on a branch and not merged: optimal L1 placement without balancing did not reduce reader-visible defects and cost 1.65× per solve.

    Along the ranks: gaps and label room

    Each layer's x origin is the previous layer's plus its width, a separation and the larger of two charges (step_layers, size.cpp:640-774):

    layer_x[r] = layer_x[r−1] + width[r−1] + sep + max(label_gap, lanes)

    Here sep is rank_sep (576), or the route clearance (96) next to a layer holding only boundary nodes or seated pseudostates; label_gap is phase 1's label charge; and lanes is turning × line height (269) where two or more edges actually turn at that boundary. An edge whose ends overlap across the ranks runs straight and takes no lane (size.cpp:486-660). Across the ranks, each end's extent grows by leader + label height; a labelled leg inside one column, or one passing a column to a folded piece, gets room on one side (§11.9.5).

    Folding long rank runs

    A frame's run of layers can be cut into pieces that are then packed or stacked like rectangles; a strip of 16 nested 15-chains would otherwise be a million units wide (§11.4; size.cpp:1324-1856).

    • Target width: max(widest layer, isqrt(area · dar_num / dar_den)), where area sums each layer's (width + rank_sep + gap) × height.
    • Cut before layer r where the running width would pass the target, or at a pinned FoldPin layer. A cut is refused where it would part an initial or final pseudostate, or a boundary node, from the node it joins.
    • Three candidates: the flat run, the folded pieces packed by pack_best, and the pieces stacked at the leading edge. The scale measure picks, unless the frame's rule is Always or Never.
    The scale measureSM = min(dar_num / (dar_den · w), 1 / h): how large the drawing can be scaled inside a viewport of the desired aspect ratio (DAR). Larger is better. It is held as a rational and compared by cross-multiplication; ties go to the smaller area, then the closer aspect (sm_tiebreak reverses that order) (pack.cpp:409-448).

    A fold whose pieces pack back into one row is not taken, and a frame running down never folds. Label room survives a fold: the label charge a cut discards rides the new piece's leading edge where the packing puts it beside the previous piece (§11.9.3). The cut fires on 59 of the corpus's 62 components; packing the pieces rather than stacking them took corpus Tier 2 down 5.6% and brew's area from 35.7M to 28.9M (§11.4).

    Packing sibling submachines

    Packing happens at three sites, all through pack_best (size.cpp:77-100): a frame's components (gap node_sep), a fold's pieces (node_sep) and a state's sibling submachines, the regions of a concurrent state (sub_sep, 192). States inside a frame are layered, never packed.

    • LR-rectpacking (Domrös et al., IVAPP 2021) sets a target width max(widest, isqrt(Σ(w+sep)(h+sep) · num / den)), then gives each rect, in order, one of four spots relative to its predecessor, the first that fits the target: Level (a new block at the row's top, tried only when the cursor sits in a lower subrow), Right, Subrow, Row. The geometry is a pure function of that spot list (pack.cpp:164-184). Reading order is placement order by construction.
    • Compaction (Level 2 bit 1) gives each rect one chance to take one of the other three spots, kept only if neither extent grows and the result is tighter (pack.cpp:196-235).
    • Whitespace elimination is always on: each row grows to the drawing's width, each block to its row's height, each subrow to its block's width and each rect to its subrow's height, slack floor-apportioned so the shares sum exactly. Extents do not change, so it never changes a comparison; only the sibling-submachine site writes the grown rects back (pack.cpp:253-328).
    • pack_box, the older packer, puts everything in one row. With trybox = 1, every pack_best call also tries it and keeps it if it fits and wins on the scale measure. Level 2 bit 0 flips trybox.

    The ratio a packing aims at is the profile's DAR (16:10 at readable, 4:3 at compact) or, on Level 2 rows with bit 2 set, the owner's hole: the state's interior between its text bands, reduced into [1, 1024] (size.cpp:2694-2731), which sizes the chart twice. Every packing is checked against COORD_MAX first, so a better-scoring packing that does not fit never displaces one that does.

    Bottom-up to the root

    A composite state's box comes from its packed submachines (§11.4; size.cpp:2217-2236):

    w = max(min_w, packed_subs_w, kind_min_w) + 2·pad
    h = max(h_before + packed_subs_h + h_after, kind_min_h) + 2·pad

    pad (128) is the interior ring only. A bare pseudostate takes no ring ("glyph == box"), so an arrow stops on the mark, not a pad short of it. At readable, a plain state is at least 896 × 640, an initial or final 224 × 224, a choice 320 × 320, a fork or join bar 64 × 960 (swapped in a frame running down).

    Phase 2's chart rect is the root submachine's. After routing, cover_chart grows it over every route point and placed label before scoring, so area and aspect price the canvas that ships (layout.cpp:429-449). A candidate copies every frame and state whose inputs, and whose descendants' inputs, match the incumbent's: 84.5% of frames are copied.

    RejectedTop-down layout, which approximates sizes from above: its size approximation is unsolved and per-level scale factors break port-split continuity (§11.4). VPSC: coordinates are generated, not adjusted (§11.13). Plain rectpacking: its oversized-child special case was deleted by its own authors, so scav takes the LR variant. OwnerHole, compaction and fold-always are Level 2 rows, not defaults: the whole chart's cost weighs them.

    PRD drift: §11.4's "every node in a layer shares that layer's x origin" and "height = max Σ heights" describe the textbook composition; in code the height comes from BK's centres and the alignment rules move nodes. box_sub (a submachine's space request) is validated and hashed but not read by sizing.

    Phase 3

    Routing: ports, faces, A*, seats and lanes

    Phase 3 draws every segment as an axis-aligned polyline between the boxes phase 2 placed. Axis-aligned is a hard constraint and states are obstacles, so a route through a box is not penalised: it cannot be represented at all (§11.5).

    In order (route.cpp:213-805): face pins become a per-segment-end table; each segment's corridor bends are gathered (phase 1's bend nodes, in route order); every net (one routed piece of a transition, one per segment) is planned and its port slots emitted; nets are batched by frame and the frames are routed in parallel, each building its region and obstacles, reusing a cached answer if the frame is unchanged (translated if it moved), else running the router and nudging that frame. The results are merged in frame order, each transition's nets are joined end to end, PathClear trims are applied, the composed polylines are nudged again chart-wide, and labels are placed last.

    Ports and the facing pass

    A port slot is where a route crosses a composite's border: on the crossed box's own border, at the boundary node's coordinate (slot_of, route.cpp:309-352). In a frame running across, rank-border ports sit on the left (leading, a source) or right (trailing, a sink), cross-border ports on the top or bottom; a frame running down swaps them. Sides are numbered 0 left, 1 right, 2 top, 3 bottom.

    Before routing, after the first sizing, the facing pass (layout.cpp:282-408) turns ports toward where their routes go. A port whose far end lies on the frame's other side has its in-frame edge reversed, which moves it to the other rank border. A port on the border of the transition's own state, whose far end lies further beyond the frame across the ranks than along them, moves to the cross border that faces it (a side pin), if that state sees the border unobstructed and no other port has that side. If anything turned, phases 1 and 2 run again. A side pin already held is never turned.

    Which face an end leaves by

    Each end of a net is seated on a face of its box. The separation rule (ortho_escape_horizontal, router_orthogonal.cpp:318-331) measures how far the other end lies outside the box on each axis; the larger separation picks the axis (a tie goes to x, the layering axis) and the nearer border picks the side. It is not the distance to a point on the border: that charged an exit for the run along its own face, and sent ota's fork bar out through its 4 pt end. Switching to the separation rule took the corpus's bends from 689 to 587 (§11.5).

    Where on the face: the other end's projection onto it, held off each corner by min(max(clear, corner arc), len/2) (onto_face). Inscribed glyphs, every kind but Normal, Fork and Join (discs, diamonds, the H), take the face's midpoint.

    A face pin (FacePin) overrides the rule at one end. A pin onto a face shorter than twice the inset is declined, since every seat on it would clamp to one point (router_orthogonal.cpp:339-348). The router reports, per end, which faces would actually move the seat, so the search never scores a face move that changes nothing. Deciding both faces as a pair from the two boxes was tried: better on estop, but +8.8% Tier 2 over the corpus with nine of eleven charts worse, "so the face is a search dimension, not a rule" (§11.5).

    The orthogonal router

    The router searches a separated orthogonal visibility graph with A* (§11.5; router_orthogonal.cpp).

    • Grid. The x lines are the region's edges, each obstacle's x − clear and x + w + clear, the enclosure walls' edges and every anchor's x; the y lines likewise. Vertices are their crossings, and an edge is passable unless it cuts an obstacle grown by clear, or a wall (router_orthogonal.cpp:906-991). The grid is full, not sparse; the flat 2k-state chart routes in 215 ms. Over 218 vertices the router refuses the frame.
    • Clearance is a bumper, not a penalty. clear = max(node_sep/3, 1) = 96: "no segment comes within clear of a box" is a property of the graph, not a price.
    • Separated planes. Each vertex has a horizontal-plane copy and a vertical-plane copy, joined by an edge whose weight is the bend penalty (Wybrow et al.), so plain A* minimises length and bends together. Node = 2·vertex + plane.
    • Costs in quarter units. A move costs 4 × length; a bend 4 × rank_sep (the bend penalty is one rank_sep, 576). An end turn, turning onto or off a fixed lead or stub direction, costs one quarter less than a bend, so of two paths equal in length and bends, the one that turns at its ends wins.
    • Heuristic: 4 × Manhattan distance, plus one bend if the current plane cannot reach the goal alone, plus one end turn if the goal's plane is fixed and differs. Admissible.
    • Frontier order: the open list is totally ordered by (f, g, node), so the pop sequence is unique; it is a radix heap on f with a 4-ary heap for the entries at the least f. The expansion budget is 220.
    • Ring points. A seat on a box border is pushed out by clear to a ring point; the leg from border to ring is emitted, not searched, so it is perpendicular for free.

    Corridors. A chained segment's bend nodes are hard waypoints: the search runs leg by leg between consecutive anchors, and ortho_simplify then removes a doubling-back spur, which is why a polyline can appear not to touch its waypoint (§11.16). A corridor net keeps both end planes free. Each frame's region is its rect, covered over every planned end and bend and grown by the clearance; its obstacles are every live state overlapping the region except the frame owner's own enclosing chain, outermost only (a box contains its descendants). Endpoint states are obstacles too: the router moves those ends onto their borders. Enclosure walls keep a route inside the state it is drawn in, a band 48 units inside its border (§11.10g step 1).

    Seating passes

    Every end's seat is chosen before any net is searched, because two ends wanting one seat is a question about the pair. Five passes run in order (router_orthogonal.cpp:1322-1382):

    1. Attach: each end is seated by the separation rule (or its face pin) at the projection of the point it aims at, the far end or the first waypoint.
    2. Reface (inscribed glyphs only): a face midpoint wanted by both an arrival and a departure moves the direction with more to gain to another face; ties move departures.
    3. Align: a net between two boxes with parallel faces gets both ends on one coordinate (halfway between the centres, clamped into both faces' runs) so one straight segment fits. A leaning net, whose label room phase 2 reserved at the leading end, takes the run's low end. Corridor nets are skipped.
    4. Spread (filled boxes): ends sharing one point on one face are split by travel direction (the net running in + takes the lower seat at both its ends), a line of text apart (269) where the face has room, else min(clear, len/3); repeated until nothing moves.
    5. Separate: legs on different boxes running alongside closer than a line of text are pushed apart, half the shortfall each, along their faces (fans are exempt).

    Seating against the box centre cut arrivals meeting a departure on one point from 116 to 16; the align and spread passes then took bends from 563 to 426 (real text), shared corridor from 30,410 to 16,494, and arrowheads landing on another route's end from 16 to 0 (§11.5). The PRD lists four passes; the code runs five.

    Nudging lanes apart

    After routing, nudging (nudge.cpp) spreads routes that run alongside each other, once per frame and again chart-wide over the composed polylines.

    • Members are interior axis-aligned segments only, each with a leg on both sides to drag; horizontal members first, then vertical, re-read from the moved geometry.
    • A lane is the union of member pairs closer than gap = max(clear, em) = 192 whose extents overlap: a distance, not collinearity.
    • Order within a lane is by where each net came from (toward, read from the end lower along the lane). Bundles (nets identical from the far point to the end, a fan-in, or from the start, a fan-out) take one offset and move whole. Crossing votes: a leg leaving strictly inside another member's extent votes for the order that avoids crossing it; the order is a linear extension of the votes by Kahn's algorithm (lowest key first), or, if votes form a cycle, fewest-contradictions insertion.
    • Room comes from the region, each member's frame (one unit inside), obstacles' grown edges and each member's leg travel. The step is min(gap, window/(groups − 1)), centred and slid back toward the lane.
    • known_good: a displacement is taken only if no leg collapses or turns round, no obstacle (or its bumper) is newly entered, no new run along a border appears, and no new shared run with another net; one refusal leaves the whole bundle where it was. "A diagram that scores well and overlaps a box is worth less than one that scores badly and does not" (§11.5).

    Without nudging, shared corridor over the corpus (no-text) was 355,116; with it, 93,066. The crossing votes then took crossings from 104 to 85 with bends unchanged at 587 (§11.5). The nudge pitch is one em (192); seats use the line height (269).

    Trims, failures and the inflation retry

    PathClear{src, dst} shortens the joined route's first and last legs to leave room for arrowheads, each capped at half its leg (route.cpp:39-50, 741-746). A net can fail three ways (router.h:67-72): OutsideRegion (an anchor outside the region), TooLarge (the grid is over budget, failing every net in the frame) and Unreachable: no path on the clearance grid and none on a tight grid with clearance 0. Success on the tight grid is a re-seat, not a failure. A degraded net is drawn as a straight line between its raw ends (box centres) through its waypoints, with one RouteDegraded diagnostic per transition.

    Only Unreachable triggers the inflation retry (layout.cpp:592-631): rank_sep, node_sep and sub_sep grow by 32 (2 pt) on a copy of the profile, cumulatively, and phases 2 and 3 run again over the same ordering, up to 8 times. The attempt that degraded least is kept (ties to the earliest), stopping at the first with nothing unreachable. The cost is always scored under the caller's profile, and Level 1 never accepts a candidate that inflated: "a move that only fits once the whole chart's spacing was widened is not a better placement, it is a bigger drawing." The corpus and both 2k shapes inflate zero times.

    One end, four faces

    The face is a search dimension. The figure below lays out estop (no text) with each of the four face pins at both ends of two transitions, each a full re-derivation of ordering, sizing and routing.

    RejectedPricing a flush lane instead of a bumper: it needs a constant tuned against the bend penalty and is only probably right. Raising the clearance to a whole em fixed 12 of 89 crowded pairs and cost containment (§11.9.3). A seat-sliding nudge for terminal legs separated none of the pairs it was for and was reverted (§11.9.5). Congestion-history routing (PathFinder) and separator channels are designed, not built: nothing measured demands them. The router is swappable by name (straight and orthogonal are registered), and the bench compares every registered router over the corpus.
    Phase 3, last step

    Labels: measured, anchored, placed

    A label is a box the application measured and asked for. Layout hangs it off its own route by a short invisible leader, inside the state that holds both ends, never over a foreign state or another route.

    Measured by the application, with scav's metrics

    Measuring is the application's job, but the metrics are scav's: one implementation measures, builds and renders, so the three never disagree. A width in grid units is ceil_div(Σ advance × font size, units per em), summed in 64 bits and divided once. It rounds up, never to nearest, because "an under-sized box is a diagram that lies". A box's height is the font size times a fixed ratio (269 units for 12 pt text on readable), not the font's own vertical metrics, which disagree with each other by 10 to 20%. Kerning is ignored, which errs wide for Latin text; a missing glyph fails loudly; and there is one bundled font. The wrap width is always an input: layout never re-wraps a label, so there is no height-to-width-to-placement fixpoint to chase.

    The request is a PathBox{subject, w, h, order}. Its size is an input to phase 1, which charges the label's width to the rank gap its segment spans, and phase 2 reserves room beside the leg it will hang from. Its position is an output of phase 3, decided after every route is final. Both belong to the transition's lowest common ancestor (LCA) segment: the piece of the route in the innermost submachine that holds both ends.

    The anchored model

    The box hangs off a point on its own polyline by an invisible leader of fixed length, half an em: max(font size / 2, 1), which is 96 units (6 pt) on readable. The leader runs in one of four directions (up, down, left, right), so its length is exact in integers, and ends on one of eight attachment points of the box: bottom-mid, top-mid, right-mid, left-mid, then the four corners. Side midpoints come first so that a tie prefers a box centred over its leg; corners are what a bend needs and come last. The candidates are:

    • every axis-aligned leg of the route that lies in the LCA frame (legs inside the states the route leaves or enters by are dropped, and diagonal legs skipped),
    • × every slide position along that leg, one every max(h / 2, 1) units, with both ends included,
    • × the 4 leader directions × the 8 attachment points. The box's origin is the slide point plus the leader minus the attachment point.

    Because the leader may run along the leg, a box can sit flush against its own leg, anywhere from 0 to one leader away.

    Rules, in two tiersBoth tiers: the box lies inside its holder, the chart intersected with every state that encloses both ends (and with the region, when the LCA is one region of a concurrent state); no leg of its own route cuts it; and it does not overlap the two states its route leaves and enters that frame by. The strict tier adds: no overlap with any wall (a live state that does not enclose both ends, endpoints included; the enclosing states' text bands; boxes already placed), nor with another transition's legs. Touching is not overlapping.

    Among the candidates that pass, the winner is the lexicographic minimum of (shortfall, dist, leg, attach, lead, slide):

    • shortfall = max(0, gap to its own leg + h − gap to the nearest foreign leg), with gaps measured as Chebyshev distance. A box closer to a neighbour's line than to its own reads as the neighbour's label, so it crosses to the far side of its own leg instead.
    • dist = the Manhattan distance from the box's centre to the anchor: the midpoint of the route's longest horizontal leg, or of its longest leg if none is horizontal.

    Fallback. If no candidate passes the strict tier, the best loose one wins: anchored, inside its holder, uncut by its own route, but allowed over a state, a band, a placed box or a foreign route. It "keeps the anchor and accepts a collision". If nothing passes at all, or the route is missing, the box is centred on the anchor and counted as unplaced. A transition with several boxes places them in order, each on legs at or after the previous one, further along the route.

    Labels in the cost

    A placed label over a foreign state (label_over_box) or over another transition's route (label_over_route) is Tier 0: forbidden outright rather than priced, so the search discards any drawing with one. The composite-endpoint exemption applies: when one endpoint encloses the other, as in On -> On/Idle, the label lives inside that endpoint, so only its text bands count against it. An ordinary endpoint is not exempt. A label over another label, or over the text bands of the states it lives in, stays in Tier 2 (label, weight 768), and the shortfall quantity is Tier 2 as label_near (weight 48). At real text every corpus chart and all 28 element charts ship with Tier 0 at zero.

    Rejected along the wayLabel dummy nodes in the layering (the textbook method), which double every rank; boxes on fixed strips at 0 to 4 box heights from the line, which sat axis's twist release seven text heights from its leg; rip-up-and-reroute for unplaceable labels, no longer needed since the loose tier; and holding "nothing between a label and its line" as a hard rule, which took fallbacks from 5 to 43 for no gain. Pruning must use the strict tier's bound: pruning by the loose one pushed boxes into the fallback, 86 corpus defects against 60.
    What scav optimises

    The objective: three tiers, compared in order

    Every drawing scav considers gets one score, a Cost. The search keeps whichever drawing has the least cost, so the cost decides what "better" means.

    A cost is a triple (t0, t1, t2). Two costs are compared lexicographically: the lower t0 wins outright; if the two t0 are equal, the lower t1 wins; only then does t2 decide. There are no multipliers between tiers. A large weight inside one sum is a cost cliff: it breaks local search, and it can overflow. Cost is computed from the finished geometry alone (state rectangles, route points, placed label boxes) and never by laying the chart out again.

    The tests are strict. Two rectangles overlap only if their interiors meet, so touching does not count. A route segment's rectangle has zero thickness, so a label box that only touches a leg costs nothing. Two segments cross only properly: a shared endpoint or a collinear overlap is not a crossing.

    Tier 0: forbidden, not priced

    t0 is the sum of eight counts. Each one counts something a reader must never see. Because Tier 0 is compared first, one violation outweighs any Tier 2 total. Most of these are already impossible by construction (the router treats states as obstacles), so Tier 0 is a safety net: for degraded routes, for the search's own trial drawings, and for the label placer's fallback.

    countcharged perwhat it forbids
    through_boxroute segment × live state it enters, unless that state encloses the route's source or destination (or is one of them)an edge drawn through an unrelated box
    box_overlappair of sibling states (children of one submachine) whose rectangles overlapboxes on top of each other
    vanishedtransition with a segment to draw whose route has fewer than 2 pointsa missing arrow. Every Tier 2 term would score an undrawn route as perfect.
    flushaxis-aligned segment lying along any state's border, within 47 units (just under 3 pt)a route the reader cannot tell from a border
    through_regionsegment entering a region (a non-root submachine) that neither end lies insidean arrow cutting through a concurrent region it has no business in
    retraceroute vertex where an axis-aligned leg turns straight back along the one beforeone run drawn twice, which reads as two routes
    label_over_boxplaced label box × state it overlaps, except states enclosing both ends and the host (an endpoint that encloses the other end); +1 if the box overlaps the host's name banda label sitting on a box
    label_over_routeplaced label box × segment of another transition's route it overlapsa label sitting on someone else's line

    The last two moved from Tier 2 into Tier 0 on this branch. At real text, every corpus chart and all 28 gauntlet charts ship with t0 = 0.

    Tier 1: hints

    t1 is meant to be an unsatisfied-hint count, weighted by priority, for an author's layout hints. Hints are not built yet, so t1 is always 0. It is compared second, so when hints arrive they will outrank everything in Tier 2.

    Tier 2: thirteen weighted terms

    t2 is a plain integer sum. Each raw term is first converted to a unit. Counts stay counts. Lengths are divided by the em, the font size in grid units: 192 (12 pt) at the shipped readable profile. Areas are divided by em² (36,864). The division rounds up. Then the term is multiplied by its weight. Grid units are 1/16 pt.

    #termraw quantityunitweight
    1bendsroute vertices where the direction changescount512
    2corridorlength two different transitions' segments share on one line, except the trunk: the final leg into a common destination (and the leg merging into it)em48
    3crossingsproper crossings between different transitions' segmentscount512
    4excess_lenper route: max(0, length − max(chord, its label widths)) × (1 + its crossings)em4
    5adjacencysegments joining two concurrent regions that are not adjacent (fork and join edges exempt)count16
    6labeloverlapping pairs of placed label boxes, plus a box over the name band of a state enclosing both endscount768
    7label_nearper box of height h: max(0, d_own + h − d_other), with d the gap to its own nearest leg and to the nearest foreign legem48
    8aspect|w·10 − h·16| of the chart, against 16:10em2
    9areaw × h of the chartem²1
    10crowdingper pair of parallel segments of different transitions overlapping by along, 0 < apart < em: along × (em − apart) / emem512
    11lengthsum of every route's polyline lengthem8
    12transit_bendsbends inside a state the route only passes through, charged on top of bendscount768
    13whitespaceper composite: interior between its text bands, less its children's areasem²0

    Crowding is continuous with corridor. At apart = 0 two segments are collinear and corridor charges them. As they separate, crowding's charge falls linearly to zero at one em. whitespace is measured but ships at weight 0. Every weight is capped at 1,024, and with the em scaling the sum stays below 254.

    Weights are exchange rates

    Because each term has its own unit, a weight says how much of one defect the reader would trade for another. At readable, one bend costs the same as one crossing. That equals one em of two lanes touching (crowding), 64 em of route length, and 512 em² of canvas (a square about 271 pt on a side). A label overlap costs 1.5 bends, and a transit bend costs 2.5 bends in total.

    Before scav scored each term in its own unit, area made up 99.48% of t2. Counts are degree 0 in the coordinates, lengths degree 1 and area degree 2, so every other term rounded to nothing. Bends fell 15% and crossings 12% while t2 moved only 0.35%. After the em conversion, the weights were fitted to pick, from 21 charts × 8 rows, the drawing with the fewest defects a reader counts: w_bends went from 64 to 512, w_label from 24 to 768, and w_area was pinned at 1. w_crowding, w_transit_bends, w_crossings and w_length were set later by hand sweeps.

    Shares

    cost_shares reports each weighted term's share of t2 in basis points, rounded down, so a row sums to just under 10,000. They are committed per chart beside the cost goldens, so a reviewer sees which defects a weight change bought and sold.

    RejectedScoring per frame: pieces leave their frame's rectangle (13 of axis's 49), so the whole chart is scored at once. Penalising excess_len heavily: it pulls against area, so it rewards sprawl. An attraction term that rewards routes for running together: the optimiser satisfies it by drawing one edge on top of another. Raising a weight ceiling to fix a scale mismatch: the ceiling is what keeps the sum inside 64 bits.
    How a drawing is found

    The search: rows, moves and kicks

    scav does not lay a chart out once. It lays it out thousands of times, each time with slightly different inputs, and ships the cheapest drawing. The search is three nested levels, all deterministic, with no randomness anywhere.

    The search rests on one fact: a drawing is a pure function of (row, pins). A row is one setting of four whole-chart knobs for sizing. A pin is one recorded decision that phases 1 to 3 must honour: hold a state at a rank, or make a route leave by a given face. There are seven kinds of pin (SearchPins): rank, cut, reverse, face, orient, side and fold. Pins are inputs to layout, not patches to its output. So trying a move means laying out again with one more pin, and undoing it means laying out with the pins held before. There is no transaction and no rollback. Pins name states and transitions by id, never by node index: chaining renumbers nodes, and an undo keyed by node silently did nothing.

    The same fact gives a counterfactual. scav dump --layout prints what a drawing rests on, for example --portfolio-row 0 --rank 11:1 --rank 0:0 --reverse 1:0 --face 3:0:1:0 --orient 2 for brew. --no-search with those flags reproduces the drawing exactly. Edit one flag to get the drawing a reader wants, then score it on the shipped objective. If it comes out cheaper, the search lacks a move. If it comes out dearer, the objective is wrong.

    Level 2: sixteen rows

    Level 2 is a fixed table of 16 rows. Row i is the profile with four bits of i flipped:

    bitknob01what it changes
    0box packeras the profile says (readable also tries the one-row box packer and keeps it if it scores better)flipped (LR-rectpacking alone)how components, fold pieces and sibling submachines are packed
    1compactionoffonLR-rectpacking's compaction step: each rectangle tries the other three spots and keeps one that does not grow the extent
    2ratio sourceprofile (every frame packs toward 16:10)owner's hole (each frame packs toward its owner's interior aspect)the aspect each frame aims for
    3foldfold where the scale measure prefers itfold wherever a run wrapswhether long rank runs fold into pieces

    Row 0 is the profile as given. The 16 rows are laid out in parallel on the thread pool, each row's layout single-threaded inside it. Every row is scored under the caller's profile, so all rows compare on one scale. If row 0 is not viable, the run fails.

    Every viable row is searched to convergence, through Level 1, kicks and the refold search. The pick is argmin(converged cost), with ties going to the lower row. Picking by starting cost is wrong. On bottler, the row with the best start (125,283) converges to 77,441. Row 0 starts worse (154,348) but converges to 51,281; the row with the best start ends 51% dearer.

    Level 1: steepest descent over pins

    The incumbent is the current best (row, pins) and its cost. A round of Level 1 lists every move the incumbent allows. Each candidate is the incumbent's pins plus one more, laid out through phases 1 to 3 and scored exactly. The round scores all of them in parallel, then reduces in enumeration order and takes the single best strictly improving move. Ties go to the earliest index. A candidate that is not viable, or that needed the spacing inflation retry, is never taken. Taking a move appends its pin and lays out the new incumbent. The search stops when a round is empty or nothing in it improves.

    moveoffered forits pinwhy it exists
    cuteach segment phase 1 chained through bend nodesChainCut: route it freely, not through its waypoints58 of 257 transitions carry a phase-1 bend, and they hold 70% of all kinks
    reverseeach segment on a cycle in its frame, not already pinnedReversePin: turn it before cycle breaking, so another edge of the cycle takes the breakwhich edge breaks a cycle decides ranks and chaining. On estop it took Tier 2 from 3,073 to 1,502 (historical objective).
    faceeach leg end of a transition whose route bends or is charged crossings, corridor, crowding, excess or a label term (every end while Tier 0 is broken), × 4 facesFacePin: leave or enter by left, right, top or bottoma local face rule cannot see the turn it buys
    sideeach leg end whose port sits on a state's border, × the other 3 sidesSidePina route arriving from above can then enter from above (axis: 5,685 → 4,645, bends 3 → 1)
    rankeach live, non-initial state, × every other rank of its frameRankPin: hold it at that rank (emptied ranks are squeezed out)which column a state sits in. Rank moves were the first ever to change a state's rank, and they take 68.5% of the search's gross gain.
    fold (refold search only)each frame drawn foldedFoldPin: which rank the single cut falls beforewhere a fold cuts (toolchanger 11,810 → 11,559)

    The budget is one counter per move kind, each capped at portfolio_k = 1,024, cumulative over the whole search. The search runs while any counter is under budget. The counters are separate because one shared budget let the first-enumerated kind starve the others: on axis, cuts then ranks under one shared budget of 24 reached 12,702, while separate counters reached 9,940. A face move whose pin cannot change the route is charged to the budget but not scored, since it would draw the incumbent exactly.

    Kicks: iterated local search

    Greedy descent stops in the first basin it finds. Some structural choices only pay off once the search has adapted to them. On estop, when kicks were built, the right reversal scored 3,218 alone, worse than the incumbent's 3,073, so a strictly improving pass never took it; accepted and searched on, it reached 1,502. (Those are the numbers of that day's objective; the drawing ships today at 906.) Simulated annealing's uphill moves were rejected because there is no temperature to calibrate. Instead, a kick applies a perturbation, searches to convergence, and keeps the result only if the converged cost is cheaper.

    • Kick kinds. Reversal: reverse each cyclic segment not already reversed. Orient: turn a frame of two or more ranks to run down the page. Fold: flip whether a frame of two or more ranks is drawn folded, if it has no fold pin. Orient and fold are allowed only in rounds "with turns".
    • Each kick takes a warm start: the incumbent's pins minus the kicked frame's rank, cut, face, side and fold pins, keeping reversals and orientations. It adds the kick's pin and runs a Level 1 search scoped to that frame. All kicks of a round run in parallel.
    • Round reduction. For each frame, keep its best kick that strictly beats the incumbent, and note the best overall (single). If two or more frames have winners, together puts every winner on one warm start, searches the union of their frames, and is taken if it beats single. Otherwise single is taken, and then each other frame's winner, cheapest first, is rested on top: searched again on the new incumbent and taken if it still improves. Rounds repeat until no kick improves. One unscoped settle search finishes.
    • Two schedules run from each row's converged drawing. A allows turns from the start. B runs reversals alone until they converge, then allows turns. B is kept only if strictly cheaper. Neither dominates: A alone shipped ota a third dearer, and B alone gives up toolchanger's 7,824 → 7,620.
    • Which rows. Every viable row kicks, in parallel, except a row whose converged drawing equals an earlier row's (same t0, t2, state rectangles and route points).

    Refold, argmin and the search memo

    After the kicks, a refold search runs Level 1 again from every viable row's pins, with fold-cut moves added. A row keeps the result only if it is strictly cheaper. The run then ships argmin over the rows' converged costs.

    A Level 1 search is a function of its inputs: the objective, the row's knobs, the budget, the refold flag, the start pins in order and the scope. The search memo stores whole searches by exactly that key (up to 224 words, under one mutex, shared by the pool for one run). A hit returns the pins and cost the search reached, and lays the drawing out again from those pins. Traced runs bypass it.

    Where the gain comes from, summed over the corpus (no text / real text): the Level 2 pick before any search gives 5.2% / 2.6% of the total improvement; Level 1 from every row gives 64.6% / 68.3%; kicks and settling give 30.2% / 28.9%; the refold search gives 0.0% / 0.1% (only axis). CPU goes the other way: kicks take about 87–89% of it. Searching to convergence instead of a budget of 24 moves cut Tier 2 by 36.7% at no text and 27.4% at real text, and reader-visible audit defects fell from 60 to 46.

    What was tried and rejected

    • In-rank order moves. Adjacent swaps (transpose) improve nothing on any frame: phase-1 crossings read 0 where routed crossings read 87. Readers' crossings happen between routes, not ranks.
    • Screening rows by a short search and finishing only the best: it dropped brew's best row, whose canvas was 38% smaller. Every row is finished.
    • Turns and fold flips as greedy moves led into worse basins (a turn made ota 18% dearer; a fold took tcp 2,685 → 3,493). They are kicks instead.
    • Kick shortcuts, each measured to lose: capping a kick's depth, keeping a kicked frame's pins, screening kicks by starting cost, skipping stale kicks, folding the facing flips into the pins, deduplicating rows at the start.
    • A frame-mirror move: it reflected the wrong axis on folded frames, cost 15% more evaluations on mill, and took tcp to a basin 36% larger.
    • A sound lower bound inside the search prunes nothing, because neighbours are near-ties. (The label bound in the next section works because it bounds only the label half.)
    • Random restarts of a constructive heuristic do about 2,000× worse than guided search at equal CPU (Martí and Laguna), and generate-and-test metaheuristics manage only 6–54 candidates a second.
    Speed without changing a drawing

    Making the search fast, exactly

    The search scores hundreds of thousands of candidates per chart. Every optimisation here is exact: with or without it, every drawing comes out byte-identical, at both scales, on every corpus chart.

    RuleEach optimisation ships with a test mode. The test mode runs the unoptimised computation alongside and compares, and a planted defect proves the comparison can fail. A memo keyed on everything a step reads returns exactly what the step would compute. A sound bound discards only candidates that could never be taken.

    Measured on bottler at no text before any of this: one layout scored 213,768 candidates, and 94% of them lost. Brandes–Köpf coordinate assignment ran 19.8 million times for only 69,496 distinct graphs, because a candidate differs from the one before it in a single frame. Sizing was 82% of the time, and 57% of samples were in the allocator. The fixes below all exploit the same fact: a candidate is the incumbent plus one pin, so almost everything it computes has been computed before.

    A general lower bound does not help inside the search. Area after sizing and a bend floor never reach 80% of the incumbent's Tier 2 on any candidate, while 58% of losers land within 1% of it. Local-search neighbours are near-ties. The label bound below works because it bounds only the label half of the cost.

    Frame memos and interned keys

    A frame is one submachine laid out as its own layered graph. It is the unit of ordering, sizing and reuse. Each thread keeps three memos (caches keyed on every value a step reads): Brandes–Köpf keyed on the whole graph; each frame's sizing, keyed on its nodes, edges, gaps, state sizes, port offsets, labels, ratio, compaction, fold and profile; and each frame's ordering, keyed on the frame as built, the pins inside it, its label charges and the profile. A memo hit emits no trace, so traced runs bypass them. Each per-thread memo is capped at 220 words (4 MiB). The memos took mill from 506 s to 58 s wall at no text on 12 cores, and bottler from 18.4 s to 2.9 s.

    The keys were later interned. A decomposed graph carries a process-unique serial for itself and its chart, so an ordering key names a frame by (serial, index) instead of spelling the frame out. The profile is one interned word instead of 52. Each transition's label segment is a table on the graph instead of a walk up the tree per box per pass. That saved 6.7% of instructions at real text.

    Per-frame ordering and sizing reuse

    Even a memo hit has to build and hash a key. Ordering reuse skips that. An ordering records what each frame reads beyond the graph: the profile; each segment's reversal, cut and side pins and label charge; each state's rank pin; and each frame's orientation. A candidate compares its record to the incumbent's frame by frame, before and after the facing pass, orders only the frames that differ, and copies the rest with node indices shifted. No key is built and no memo is probed.

    Sizing reuse does the same for coordinates, with one difference: sizing runs bottom-up, since a frame's size depends on its children's. So a candidate marks every frame whose inputs differ and every frame that holds it, deepest first, and copies the rest. Over the corpus and gauntlet, 84.5% of frames are copied, and instructions fell 6.1% at real text.

    The face shortcut

    Phases 1 and 2 and the facing pass never read a face pin, and face moves were two thirds of all scored moves. So a face candidate is routed and scored starting from the incumbent's kept phase-1 and phase-2 state, at about a quarter of the cost of a rank candidate (65 µs against 252 µs on mill). It also keeps the incumbent's labels wherever nothing a box reads has changed: 92% of a face move's boxes on mill.

    Two refinements followed. No-op faces are charged, not scored. The router reports, per route end, which faces would actually move the seat. A face pin elsewhere draws the incumbent exactly, so it is charged to the budget without being scored. That is about a quarter of face moves. Faces are offered only where they are priced. A route end's four faces are offered only if its transition's route bends, or is charged crossings, corridor, crowding, excess length or a label term, or at every end while the incumbent breaks Tier 0. The incumbent's own scoring fills this mask, once per taken move, never per candidate. At real text every drawing stayed byte-identical, only 48% of face candidates are scored, and instructions fell 16.4%.

    The label bound: route first, label best-first

    Labels are placed last and read only the routes. So before any label is placed, every route term, adjacency and the six route-only Tier 0 counts are already final. A round with labels runs in two passes:

    1. Route every candidate in parallel without labels and score a lower bound. The label terms are zero, area and whitespace are measured over the unlabelled chart, and aspect is dropped unless every label box fits inside the sized chart.
    2. Visit the candidates whose bound beats the incumbent, least bound first (ties by enumeration index). Place labels and score each exactly, but only while its bound can still beat the best exact cost so far, or tie it at a lower index. Stop at the first that cannot.

    The pick is exactly what scoring every candidate whole would give, and a test mode scores every bounded round whole and compares. At real text, 91% of candidates never place their labels, and instructions fell 35.5% (mill 4,002 G → 2,613 G). Two variants lost: keeping every candidate's routes saved 5% more instructions but cost 16% more memory, and labelling 8 or 32 at once cost 5–11% more.

    Kept bound geometry. The first pass already routed each candidate, so routing it again for the exact pass is waste. A candidate whose bound is below the incumbent keeps its routes while it is among the 128 least by (bound, index), in a per-search slot swapped with the scorer's scratch so that nothing allocates. Its exact pass restores the chart those routes saw and places labels on them instead of laying out again. On mill, the 128 slots cover 92% of the candidates that get labelled, and save 4.5% of instructions at the same peak memory. Keeping every candidate's routes saves 4.6% but costs 35–42% more memory.

    Allocation-free scratch

    Ordering, sizing and packing, scored-move pins and candidates, routes, label placement, nudging and coordinate views all fill per-thread buffers that are reused across candidates. On bottler at real text, heap allocations per scored candidate fell 216 → 103 → 53 → 14 → 8.7 → 4.2, and allocations over a whole run fell from 72.2 M to 1.39 M. Ordering scratch is kept per nesting depth, because a thread waiting on a call's shards may itself run a candidate that orders.

    The radix A* queue

    The router's A* pops nodes in (f, g, node) order, which is a strict total order. So any exact priority queue pops the same sequence. The open list is now a radix heap over f. Entries at the least f sit in a 4-ary heap on the whole order. A push below the current least lowers it and re-places every entry, because the heuristic is admissible but not consistent at the turn into a fixed end. It executes about 1% more instructions but takes 4–6% fewer cycles (mill real text 834 G → 786 G cycles). Route lengths need a square root, and hardware sqrt is banned for determinism. The integer square root now runs Newton's method from above, starting one shift-only step from the nearest power of two and stopping at the first step that does not fall. It is checked exhaustively over all 32-bit inputs and cut 2.5% of mill's instructions.

    One global thread pool

    All parallel work goes to one pool. The first free thread takes the lowest unclaimed shard of the deepest open job. Nested calls (rows, then searches, then candidate rounds) push to the same pool, so no call site has to divide the host's cores among its children. One bottler search went from 755% to 1,085% of 12 cores. A hierarchical profile shows 8.7–11 of 12 cores busy, idle 3.5–4.4%, and 0.2% of time in locks.
